title: What the Fig Tree Withheld for Seven Years
script: Narrator: [reflective] My grandfather planted a fig tree the year I was born, a gesture I understood, for most of my childhood, as merely sentimental rather than instructive.
Narrator: [honestly] For seven consecutive years, that tree produced nothing worth mentioning, a handful of shriveled, inedible fruit that fell before ripening and rotted quietly in the grass.
Narrator: [thoughtful] My grandfather never once proposed uprooting it, despite my father's periodic suggestion that the space might be better allocated to something more obliging.
Narrator: [with feeling] He simply kept tending it, pruning with an almost liturgical patience, as though barrenness were a phase to be outlasted rather than a verdict to be accepted.
Narrator: [honestly] I asked him once, with the impatience peculiar to adolescence, why he bothered persisting with something so stubbornly unproductive.

Narrator: [reflective] He told me that a tree owes nothing to a calendar, that fruitfulness arrives on a timeline utterly indifferent to our impatience, and that uprooting it prematurely would only guarantee the harvest never came.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I didn't fully register the weight of that answer then, filed it away as one of his characteristically cryptic pronouncements, and largely forgot it.
Narrator: [with feeling] The eighth summer, inexplicably, the tree surrendered an abundance so sudden it seemed almost to mock the years of apparent failure preceding it.

Narrator: [gently] Watching him gather that first proper harvest, I understood, belatedly, that he'd never actually been waiting on the tree at all. He'd been demonstrating something considerably larger about patience itself.

Narrator: [reflective] I think of that fig tree often now, whenever some effort of mine yields nothing for longer than seems reasonable, whenever I'm tempted toward the premature verdict that barrenness is final.
Narrator: [with a small smile] My grandfather has been gone a decade, but that tree still bears fruit every summer, and every summer I remember precisely what it was actually teaching me all along.

quiz.question: How did the narrator initially understand his grandfather's gesture of planting the fig tree?
options: As a practical business investment
As merely sentimental rather than instructive
As a religious obligation
As a competition with neighbors
quiz.explanation: He understood it, for most of his childhood, as merely sentimental rather than instructive.

quiz.question: What did the narrator's father periodically suggest?
options: That the tree needed more water
That the space might be better allocated to something more obliging
That the tree should be sold
That the grandfather should plant more trees
quiz.explanation: His father periodically suggested the space might be better allocated to something more obliging than the barren tree.

quiz.question: What did the grandfather say about a tree's relationship to a calendar?
options: Trees always follow a predictable calendar
A tree owes nothing to a calendar; fruitfulness arrives on its own timeline
Trees should be replaced if they miss a season
Calendars are irrelevant to farming
quiz.explanation: He said a tree owes nothing to a calendar, and fruitfulness arrives on a timeline indifferent to human impatience.

quiz.question: What happened in the eighth summer?
options: The tree died completely
The tree surrendered an abundance so sudden it seemed to mock the years of apparent failure
The tree produced the same small amount as before
The family finally uprooted it
quiz.explanation: In the eighth summer, the tree inexplicably produced an abundance so sudden it seemed to mock the prior years of failure.

quiz.question: What did the narrator realize his grandfather had actually been demonstrating?
options: How to grow figs efficiently
Something considerably larger about patience itself, not just waiting on the tree
How to argue with his son
The uselessness of gardening
quiz.explanation: He realized his grandfather had never simply been waiting on the tree, but demonstrating something larger about patience itself.
